Cautiously positive, but further tempered by credit-supply and demand signals from the SLOOS. While the FOMC notes strong labor markets and solid household spending, the SLOOS indicates softer business-side dynamics that align with weak business fixed investment and exports:
- Weaker demand for C&I loans reported by foreign banks, and weaker demand in construction and land development loans; demand was unchanged in some CRE segments (nonfarm nonresidential, multifamily).
- Some tightening of lending standards for C&I, with “economic outlook” and “liquidity” cited as reasons; any easing was largely competition-driven rather than fundamentals-driven.

These SLOOS findings reinforce a risk-aware stance: easy financial conditions and Fed actions (T-bill purchases, repo operations) help ensure ample reserves and support transmission, but softer business loan demand and some tightening in standards suggest capex sensitivity and potential drag from credit channels. Coupled with previously flagged financial stability vulnerabilities (elevated corporate leverage, nonbank intermediation links, and liquidity fragilities), the outlook remains mildly positive but more guarded than the FOMC statement alone would imply.
